newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Web site spreads the "good news".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Web site spreads the "good news".

text.p: If the credo of mainstream media is "if it bleeds, it leads," then publisher John Groom is here to say there is "good news every day."

That is the idea behind Groom's Web site Positive Press, run from his nonprofit organisation, The Athens Institute in Alexandria, Virginia. Positive Press was founded on the World Wide Web in July "to counteract the tendency of the mainstream media to focus on the negative," its mission statement says.
Within four days of its appearance, Positive Press was selected by online service Yahoo as a pick of the week, Pacific Bell has made it an educational link and it has logged 200,000 hits to date.

On a typical day, his research team of two ploughs through the Internet and culls this good news: from the Detroit News, Chrysler has donated $2 million to the Detroit Symphony Orchestra; from the Arizona Star, chocolate may be the next health food; from Reuters, Shannon Lucid comes home from the shuttle after logging the most time in space for a woman; and from CNN, Dan, a springer spaniel that had taken a water rescue class, is credited with saving the life of a toddler.

The Hartford Courant has the story of a man who found some 40-year-old dynamite, still explosive, in his garage. "If he had dragged, rather than carried, that package, this would not be a Positive Press story," the group crows.

A "historical perspective section" gives the long view on the accomplishments of humankind. This week's antidote to tragedy: Travel by plane is safer than it was a generation ago; in the last nine years, the odds of perishing in a commercial airliner have been one in 1.3 million.
In his online statement of philosophy, Groom cites Plutarch. And a thought of the day is from Emerson: "Go with mean people, and you think life is mean."
Groom, 35, was a real estate developer when boom turned to bust. "I kept trying to think, 'Things are not really that bad. You've got to keep perspective,'" he said.

"I would look around for upbeat news. By the time I had found something like that, I would have to have read eight stories about a gang shooting or a hurricane in China or a volcanic eruption where 20 people had been killed -- the very negative things that the media tend to cover because people have a perverse attraction to those things," he said.

"I kept thinking, 'Wouldn't it be good if there was some place you could go to that would be an inspirational news source, where you could read the good news?' A lot of sites on the Web have a positive inclination but it's kind of in the flower child way, like 'We're all beautiful. Let's all be nice to each other.'"

Groom not only did not want to be silly, he did not want to be religious. "It's non-controversial, non-sectarian, secular," he said of his news service. He chooses bounce-back stories, stories of quiet heroism, stories about children, news about medical breakthroughs and bullish economic items.

"If you read polls, people view the world as getting worse, crime is getting worse. I don't think that's true," he said. "The world's really a lot safer than it has been in the past. It's a lot cleaner than it has been in the past. People live longer. They receive better medical care.

"There are problems in the world. No one denies this. My attitude is ... let's take a hard, cold ruthless look at reality and if you do take a hard, cold ruthless look you'll see lots of good. You don't have to be a cynic to be a realist."

Groom said he has done "zero promotions" and "zero advertising" for his site. He pays for it with his own time and money. What is in it for him? Not much, except the hope he has found an untapped market for positive press and the satisfaction of getting happy news, he said.

"I tell you when I feel especially good is when I come across a particularly good story," he said. "Like the three-year-old who fell into the gorilla's cage and the gorilla carried it to safety. That was perfect for us."
Positive Press is located at http://www.positivepress.com.
